To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the HIV-1 envelope protein is a key target for neutralizing antibodies, but the envelope protein uses several mechanisms, including the V1V 2 region, to evade the immune system.
rationally targeted mutations at V1V2 can augment virus neutralization by anti-V1V2 monoclonal antibodies.
rationally targeted mutations at the V1 and the V2 loops of the HIV- 1 envelope glycoprotein can augment the neutralizing activity of anti-V2 monoclonal antibodies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) against HIV-1 and the mechanisms of HIV-1 resistance against the bNAbs.
developing a new class of HIV-1 vaccine immunogens that can induce antibodies capable of neutralizing diverse HIV-1 isolates.
the development of a novel HIV vaccine based on the use of a highly conserved and immunogenic epitope in the V1/V2 domain of the viral envelope glycoprotein (Env).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
V1V2 is the most variable region on the surface of the HIV-2 envelope, and that it is also the most conserved.
the V2 loop is a major target for HIV-1 neutralization and that V1/V2 mutations can enhance virus sensitivity to neutralizing antibody.
the HIV-1 virus has evolved to shield the V1V1 epitopes and that this shielding is a major factor that limits the ability of V1V1 Abs to neutralize HIV-1 virus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified several key elements in the V1V1 domain that are important for antibody recognition.
we have developed a rational strategy to target the V1V3 loop of HIV-1 Env to augment virus neutralization by V1V2-directed mAbs.
we have identified a new class of HIV-1 neutralizing antibodies that are highly conserved and target the conserved integrins binding domain on the HIV-1 envelope.
The main takeaway from our work is that
multiple elements within V1V2 act independently and in an HIV-1-dependent fashion to regulate the accessibility of V2 epitopes.
the V1V3 loop is a key determinant for the occlusion of V2i antibodies.
the HIV-1 envelope protein (Env) has evolved multiple mechanisms to escape neutralizing antibody recognition, but the Env also contains conserved regions that are recognized by antibodies.
